title: Rain That Reaches Both Coasts
statement:
An island is a grid heights of land heights. The north-west sea lies along the top edge and the left edge of the grid. The south-east sea lies along the bottom edge and the right edge.

Rain that falls on a cell can flow to a neighbour that shares a side with it if that neighbour is no higher (height less than or equal). A cell on an edge drains straight into the sea on that edge. Rain keeps flowing as long as it can and may take any allowed route.

Return the coordinates [r, c] of every cell from which rain can reach both seas. Any order is accepted.

examples.why: The cell (0, 1) is on the top edge, so it reaches the north-west sea, but rain there can only run down to (0, 0), which is also stuck in the corner. Neither reaches the south-east sea. Every other cell can.
Rain flows between equal heights. Requiring a strictly lower neighbour would leave (0, 0) and (1, 1) out.
The middle cell is a pit: all its neighbours are higher, so its rain goes nowhere. The ring around it is flat and touches both seas.

hints: Following the rain from every single cell repeats a lot of work. What if you started at the sea and asked which cells could have sent water there?
Walk inland from a sea's edge cells, stepping only to neighbours that are at least as high. Every cell you reach can drain into that sea.
Do that search once from the north-west edges and once from the south-east edges. The answer is the cells marked by both.

explain.intuition:
The direct approach asks, for each cell, "where can rain from here go?" and runs a search downhill. That is one search per cell, and neighbouring cells repeat almost the same search.

Turn the arrows around. Rain can go from a to a neighbour b when b is no higher. So, starting from the sea and walking uphill (to neighbours at least as high), you reach exactly the cells whose rain can come back down to you. Every cell on the top or left edge drains into the north-west sea, so seed one search with all of them; every cell on the bottom or right edge seeds a second search. Each search visits each cell at most once. A cell marked by both searches is in the answer. The same "search backwards from the goal" trick works whenever many starts share a few targets.
steps: Seed a BFS with every cell on the top row and left column, marking them in nw. Seed another with the bottom row and right column, marking them in se.
In each BFS, from cell (r, c) step to each in-bounds neighbour that is not yet marked and whose height is at least heights[r][c], mark it and push it.
Collect every [r, c] marked in both grids.
pitfalls: Using the wrong comparison in the reversed search. Going backwards you climb: the next cell must be greater than or equal. Using less-than walks the wrong way and marks cells that cannot drain.
Using a strict comparison. Water flows across equal heights, so example 2 expects every cell.
Forgetting that a cell can sit on both seas' edges, such as the top-right and bottom-left corners. Seed each search with its own edges independently.

solutions.title: Search downhill from every cell
solutions.idea: For each cell, flood every cell its rain can reach and record which seas' edges the flood touches. Correct, but one full search per cell.

solutions.title: Climb inland from each sea
solutions.idea: Two BFS runs, each seeded with one sea's edge cells, stepping only to neighbours at least as high. Cells marked by both runs are the answer.

followups: There are four seas, one on each edge, and you want cells that reach at least three of them. How does the approach extend?
Rain may only flow to a strictly lower neighbour. Which single comparison changes?
